newsitem.title: USA: Weather may force early return of shuttle Columbia.
newsitem.headline: Weather may force early return of shuttle Columbia.

text.p: The U.S. space shuttle Columbia had to cancel a pair of spacewalks because of a stuck hatch and now may have to return to earth one day early because of bad weather forecast for landing sites on both U.S. coasts on Friday, NASA officials said on Tuesday.

The space mission was recently extended from Thursday until Friday, but rainy weather is forecast for the shuttle's prime landing site in Florida and high winds would affect the backup landing strips in California and New Mexico, mission control's Marc Garneau told the five astronauts.

"The weather folks have been continuing to assess the weather for the next few days at the Cape, and it looks as if there is a possibility that on flight day 17, which is currently your landing day, the weather may have deteriorated at the Cape," Garneau told the crew after waking them up to begin their work day.
NASA mission managers were to meet at 9 a.m. EST (1400 GMT) on Wednesday to make a final decision on whether the orbiter would return to earth on Thursday or on Friday.

"We would prefer to proceed with the orderly conduct of the remaining events of this flight, including the documentation of the (stuck) hatch conditions that have been sent up to us and shoot for a landing on flight day 17," said shuttle commander Kent Cockrell.
He said the astronauts had plenty of food, water, oxygen and fresh clothes, and "an excellent crew attitude" in case the orbiter's return was delayed beyond Friday.
The shuttle's five-member crew was scheduled early on Wednesday to recapture a star-gazing telescope, which has been trailing the shuttle through space for the past two weeks.
Thrusters will manoeuvre Columbia into place and astronaut Tom Jones will use the shuttle's robot arm to pluck the satellite from space at 3:11 a.m. EST (0811 GMT) and deposit it in the payload bay.

"The Orfeus-Spas is equipped with a grapple fixture. He'll reach out and grab the telescope," NASA spokeswoman Eileen Hawley said. But if something goes wrong with the retrieval, the retraction of antennas or the robot arm, one of the standard procedures -- a spacewalk or "extra vehicular activity" (EVA) in NASA jargon -- to fix the problem may not be an option.

The Orfeus-Spas telescope, released from the shuttle shortly after launch, has been one of the success stories of a mission marred by a jammed airlock hatch that forced the cancellation of two planned spacewalks.

On Monday, ground controllers decided to extend the mission by a day to give the telescope, a U.S.-German project, more time to gather data on interstellar matter in a study on the life cycles of stars.
The extra day meant that Columbia was scheduled to return to earth on Friday, landing at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre shortly after 8 a.m. EST (1300 GMT).

During a news conference from the shuttle late on Monday, astronaut Tammy Jernigan said if an emergency arose the crew would have to make another attempt to get the hatch open. "If we got into that very remote possibility then we would work very hard to get that hatch open and very hard to get it sealed back," she said.

But Cockrell said the possibility of an emergency spacewalk was remote because of contingencies for the failure of the payload bay doors or the robot arm. "It actually hasn't crossed our mind really that an EVA that perhaps can't be done would be required," he said.
NASA engineers remained mystified by the failure of the airlock hatch, which prevented the astronauts from leaving the shuttle on Thursday to perform their spacewalks.
